title: Making Local 3D Furniture Portable in a Vue 2 Indoor-Map SDK
summary: KiMap's indoor map SDK now enables portable 3D furniture by embedding model content and metadata directly, allowing Vue 2 applications to render furniture without external servers. The update maintains backward compatibility with existing integrations while supporting new upload-driven applications. The MIT-licensed SDK supports multiple model formats including OBJ, FBX, GLB, and glTF.
content:
An indoor map stops being portable when every chair, desk, or fixture still depends on a private model URL.
KiMap exports now keep furniture metadata in kidata.furnitures and model content in kidata.models. Each furniture item points to its embedded model through modelRef, so the Vue 2 SDK can parse OBJ, FBX, GLB, or glTF content from memory and restore position, rotation, scale, size, and material settings without a separate furniture server.
The compatibility requirement mattered just as much as the new path. Existing integrations can continue providing a .kimap URL, while upload-driven applications can pass kimapContent, kidataContent, and kithemeContent directly.
The SDK is MIT licensed:
https://github.com/zyl19950114/kimap-vue2-sdk
You can test the editor example without signing in:
https://www.kimap.cc/editor/example?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=early_access&utm_content=sdk_followup
The most useful feedback is specific: which model format, loading lifecycle, or scene-performance limit would block your integration?

title: Pacing the Frontier Shows How AI Employees Are Organizing on Safety Governance
summary: Over 1,350 employees from frontier AI companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and Meta have published a collective statement calling for coordinated government action to pace advanced AI development. The employee-led initiative, supported by independent nonprofits, frames safety governance as requiring coordination beyond individual company decisions. The effort demonstrates how employees can form a distinct constituency within the ongoing public debate over AI safety and regulation.
content:
Pacing the Frontier is a public call by employees from frontier AI companies for governments to coordinate how the most advanced AI development is paced. The initiative matters not because it sets company policy, but because it gives researchers and other employees a collective channel to argue for safety and governance measures across competing labs.
The official Pacing the Frontier statement describes itself as "A statement from 1,350 employees of frontier AI companies." It also states that employees published it with organizational support from two independent nonprofits, Guidelight AI Standards and Encode AI. That distinction is central to understanding the effort: it is employee-led, with outside organizational support, rather than a directive issued by a single AI company.
The statement calls for coordinated government action to deliberately pace frontier AI development and for technical and governance tools that could support that objective. Its signatories include people associated with multiple leading labs, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind and Meta, according to the statement and reporting cited in the supplied research. Participation is broad, but it is not the same as a uniform corporate commitment by those organizations.
Frontier AI companies increasingly face public scrutiny over how they evaluate advanced systems, communicate risk and engage with regulation. Pacing the Frontier places employees within that debate as a distinct constituency. It frames safety as an issue that can require coordination beyond the competitive decisions of any one lab.
That framing is more precise than treating the statement as an official industry policy. The available evidence supports three related, but different, conclusions:
The initiative is employee-led. The primary statement explicitly identifies its authors as employees of frontier AI companies.
Independent nonprofits provided support. Guidelight AI Standards and Encode AI are credited with organization

Different API endpoints
Separate accounts and dashboards

Your application

title: Privacy-First Healthcare: Real-time ECG Denoising with WebLLM and WebGPU 🩺⚡
summary: This guide demonstrates how to implement real-time ECG denoising directly in the browser using WebGPU and WebLLM, eliminating the need to send sensitive patient data to servers. By leveraging Transformer-based architectures, the approach enables high-throughput signal processing and arrhythmia classification at 60fps while maintaining full privacy. The zero-latency, zero-backend design addresses regulatory compliance concerns around handling sensitive biometric data.
content:
In the world of digital health, the "Cloud-First" approach is hitting a massive wall: Privacy. Sending raw, sensitive Bio-signal data like Electrocardiograms (ECG) to a central server isn't just a latency nightmare—it's a regulatory minefield. 
What if we could run heavy-duty signal processing and AI classification directly in the user's browser? Thanks to WebGPU acceleration and the maturity of Edge AI, we can now achieve zero-latency, zero-backend-cost processing. By leveraging WebLLM and WASM, we are moving the intelligence to where the data lives. In this guide, we’ll explore how to implement a real-time ECG denoising pipeline that ensures raw patient waveforms never leave the device.
Processing ECG signals requires high throughput. Traditional JavaScript is too slow for real-time Fourier transforms or deep learning inference on high-frequency (500Hz+) signals. This is where WebGPU comes in, providing a low-level interface to the device's graphics hardware.
Here is the data flow of our browser-based medical AI pipeline:
graph TD
    A[ECG Sensor/Raw Data] -->|Web Serial / File| B(TypeScript Data Buffer)
    B -->|WASM Pre-processing| C{WebGPU Pipeline}
    C -->|Quantized Model| D[WebLLM Inference Engine]
    D -->|Denoised Signal| E[Real-time Canvas Visualization]
    D -->|Classification| F[Local UI Notification]
    E --> G[Privacy Shield: No Data Sent to Server]
    F --> G

You might think WebLLM is just for chatbots. Think again. At its core, WebLLM leverages the TVM (Tensor Virtual Machine) stack to compile model weights into specialized WebGPU shaders. 
When we treat ECG signals as a time-series sequence, we can utilize Transformer-based architectures (similar to those used in LLMs) to identify patterns, filter out "powerline interference," and classify arrhythmias—all running at 60fps in Chrome or Edge.
To follow along, ensure your environment meets these requirements:
  Tech Stack: TypeScript, WebLLM (via @mlc-ai/web-llm), and a browser supporting WebG

title: Devs are adding typos to prove they're not ChatGPT and that's bleak
summary: As AI detection tools gain popularity, developers are paradoxically making their writing worse by intentionally adding typos and grammatical errors to prove their work is human-authored rather than AI-generated. A new Chrome extension called Sincerely has capitalized on this trend by offering to deliberately degrade writing quality for $4.99/month, while unreliable AI detection tools misidentify human text as machine-generated. The phenomenon highlights a perverse incentive structure where improving writing clarity now damages professional credibility.
content:
Last week someone accused me of being a robot. Can you believe it? The reviewer responded with "This reads like it was written by ChatGPT." I guess I had spent 40 seconds on that. ## The new suspicion tax
For years, we have been advising developers to improve their writing. Writing clear commits, readable comments, and documentation that does not make others cry. Writing clearly is now considered a crime. There is a whole discussion on a developer forum about this. Where people make well-structured comments and are accused of being AI. The solution it seems is to write badly on purpose then. 🙃
Developers are deliberately including typos in the code. Tiny, deliberate grammatical errors are added to show that a human wrote it and made a mistake. That's the sad reality. We are simplifying things not because we don't want to make an effort, but as a survival strategy. ## Somebody built a business on this
April 2026 saw the launch of a Chrome extension called Sinceerly, created by a Harvard Business School developer Ben Horwitz. The interesting thing about it? The name was misspelled on purpose. It is advertised as the opposite of Grammarly. Rather than correcting your writing, it breaks your writing using AI. The "Human" mode will make your text sound like it was written by a talkative human, and the "CEO" mode will make it sound like a text written by a busy top executive. Horwitz tested the tool's efficiency by sending typo-filled cold emails to five Fortune 500 CEOs. Four of them responded. After you've tried it for free, you only pay $4.99 per month to stop sounding so smart. Just think about that for a minute. We built AI to write for us. Now we pay a different AI to un-write it. ## The detectors made this worse
Here's the reason people are afraid. The tools that were intended to detect AI are extremely untrustworthy. GPTZero can incorrectly identify certain human-created paragraphs as machine-like with a rate of up to 22% in some cases. This can be quite alarming

title: Failed Webhook Retry Queues, Exponential Backoff, DLQs, and Redrive
summary: The article advocates for using a queue-plus-dead-letter-queue architecture with application-level exponential backoff for failed webhook delivery, rather than simple retry loops. The design treats the queue as a durable boundary between business state and outbound HTTP, requiring idempotency tables and append-only attempt records keyed by delivery ID. The approach ensures exactly-once business effects while tolerating at-least-once queue semantics and network failures.
content:
Short answer: Use a queue plus dead-letter queue for failed webhooks, apply application-level exponential backoff through delayed republishes, and allow manual DLQ redrive after the underlying problem is fixed; otherwise reach for a workflow engine when delivery is only one step in a durable, multi-stage process.
This is an architecture decision, not a retry-loop trick. A standard queue is at-least-once, so duplicate delivery is normal and consumer idempotency is mandatory. I design the delivery record and audit trail before I choose the queue product because a payment system that sends the same settlement notification twice has not achieved correctness merely because both HTTP calls returned 200.
The decision is to make the queue the durable boundary between business state and outbound HTTP. A producer creates a stable delivery ID, records the intended destination and payload digest, then publishes that identity to the main queue. A worker consumes it, attempts the webhook, and records the attempt before acknowledging success. A retryable failure causes a delayed republish whose delay grows exponentially; crossing the configured attempt ceiling moves the job to a DLQ. Redrive is an operator action after the receiver, payload mapping, or authentication issue has been corrected. The invariant is one business effect per delivery ID, not one network request. A standard queue can present the same message more than once, an acknowledgement can be lost, and a receiver can commit its work before the caller sees the response. The receiver therefore needs an idempotency table keyed by delivery ID, while the sender needs an append-only attempt record containing the delivery ID, attempt number, response class, timestamp, and next action. Those records are what I reconcile against the ledger. Keep the payload small and refer to durable business data by ID.
